overview.text: This Final Environmental Impact Statement evaluates the City of San Jose's second three-year Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) plan, a federally funded neighborhood improvement program running July 1978 to June 1981 that pays for housing rehabilitation loans and grants, street and sewer work, parks, and community centers in seven designated target neighborhoods — Alma, Alviso, Campus, Gardner, Mayfair, Northside, and Olinder. These neighborhoods contain the city's oldest, most deteriorated housing and are home to disproportionately low-income, elderly, and Spanish-speaking residents, including a Housing Assistance Plan estimate of 30,452 lower-income households needing housing help as of January 1978. The Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) considers rejected project proposals plus four single-category alternatives (all funds to housing rehabilitation, parks, streets, or social services) and a no-project alternative that would forgo the plan's benefits and jeopardize the partially completed San Antonio Plaza Redevelopment Project. Environmental effects are mostly short-term construction impacts — dust, noise of 84–88 dBA at 50 feet from the loudest equipment, possible disturbance of archaeological sites, and siting concerns such as expanding the Olinder Library in a flood zone and building the Alma Neighborhood Center on soils with high liquefaction potential — with generally positive long-term effects on housing quality, sewers, and groundwater. Public involvement included three City Council public hearings, a Steering Committee that reviewed 39 citizen funding proposals over nine meetings, and formal comment letters from the State Historic Preservation Officer, San Jose Parks and Recreation, and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Region IX, which rated the draft 'LO-2' (Lack of Objections on impact, Insufficient Information on the statement).

project_description.text: The document is the Final Environmental Impact Statement for the City of San Jose's Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Three-Year Plan for July 1978 through June 1981 — the second three-year cycle of federally funded neighborhood improvements authorized by the Housing and Community Development Acts of 1974 and 1977. The plan concentrates activities in seven designated Concentrated Neighborhood Revitalization Areas (target neighborhoods for coordinated upgrading): Alma, Alviso, Campus, Gardner, Mayfair, Northside, and Olinder. Typical activities include housing rehabilitation loans and grants, street reconstruction (curbs, gutters, storm and sanitary sewer lines, lights, resurfacing), construction of new parks and community centers such as the Alma Neighborhood Center, expansion of the Olinder (Carnegie) Library, and citywide projects including roughly 250 curb ramps for handicapped access and support for the San Antonio Plaza Redevelopment Project.

alternatives_overview.text: The Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) discusses specific project proposals rejected by the Steering Committee or City Council (such as an Alviso skateboard park, a Mayfair amphitheater, and a Campus John XXIII parking/housing site), four single-category alternatives that would put all Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funds into just one activity — housing rehabilitation, park acquisition and improvement, street improvements, or social services — and a no-project alternative. Each single-category alternative would avoid some negative impacts of the proposed plan but would leave other neighborhood-blight problems unaddressed; the social services alternative would produce essentially no negative environmental impacts. The no-project alternative would avoid all construction impacts but forgo the plan's benefits and leave the city with serious financial obligations from its partially completed redevelopment projects, including San Antonio Plaza.

environmental_impact.text: Most impacts are short-term construction effects: temporary increases in airborne dust (particulates) from demolition, trenching, and paving, and construction noise averaging 84 to 88 dBA at 50 feet from the loudest equipment. Mitigation includes performing dust-producing activities during the wetter months of November through April, and adding double-pane windows, weatherstripping, and insulation during rehab, which can yield up to a 30% long-term energy savings. Significant site-specific hazards include seismic risk — the Silver Creek Fault zone underlies all of developed Alviso and about half of Northside, and the maximum credible earthquake would produce ground acceleration of 0.3g to 0.35g — plus high liquefaction potential on alluvial soils in all seven target neighborhoods, and 100-year flood risk covering 100% of Alviso and Campus and 80% of Olinder. Alviso has flooded from creek overflows in 1955, 1958, 1963, and 1968, and its protective dikes were built for salt-pond retention rather than urban flood protection. Two siting concerns are noted: prolonging the life of the Olinder Library in a flood zone and constructing the Alma Neighborhood Center in an area of high liquefaction potential. Air quality is poor — the Bay Area is a federal non-attainment area for carbon monoxide and oxidants — and Mayfair has elevated carbon monoxide from Route 680. The saltmarsh north of Alviso is habitat for two endangered species, the California Clapper Rail and the Saltmarsh Harvest Mouse. Archaeologically sensitive areas in Gardner, Olinder, Mayfair, Northside, and Alviso require monitoring during trenching, and the project is expected to have no permanent impact on traffic while sewer upgrades should improve groundwater quality.

public_response.text: The city held three public hearings on the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) program, and the CDBG Steering Committee reviewed 39 citizen funding proposals across nine meetings before adopting the three-year plan; at the November 2, 1977 hearing, 25 speakers from 12 neighborhoods described specific problems including sewage backing up into houses and dangerous sidewalk differentials. At a December 19, 1977 Steering Committee meeting, members pushed back on using CDBG funds for the Redevelopment Agency's San Antonio Plaza project and questioned the need for another community center at Backesto Park. Four formal comment letters/memos were received on the Draft EIR/Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) from the State Historic Preservation Officer, the San Jose Parks and Recreation Director, a correction on the Olinder Library location, and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Region IX. EPA classified the draft as Category LO-2 — 'Lack of Objections' on environmental impact but 'Insufficient Information' on the statement — and asked for more detail on air quality, traffic capacity on Highways 101, 17, and 280, dike improvements, and flooding. The State Historic Preservation Officer flagged Santa Clara County Archaeological Site #230 near Olinder and the adjacent Alviso National Register Historic District, and asked that the twenty structures slated for demolition be assessed. The Planning Commission approved the Final EIR on April 5, 1978 by a 6-0 vote, finding no significant effect on the environment.

RESPONSE TO COMMENTS
The following are responses to comments received on the Community Development Block Grant DEIR/DEIS.
Response to comments from Dr. Knox Mellon, State of California Department of Parks and Recreation.
Comment: Santa Clara Archaeological Site #230 is located in the vicinity of the Olinder neighborhood.
Response: The site is over one mile from the project area and there does not appear to be any negative environmental reciprocity involved.
<u>Comment</u>: The Alviso National Register Historic District is adjacent to the Alviso project area.
Response: In addition to the Historic District, which is recognized by (see Summary Section K) the project, recent information has been brought to the Planning Department's attention that the Alviso area, at large, is also archaeologically sensitive (source: Arthur Ogilvie, PhD., Santa Clara County Planning Department).
The archaeological resource maps available to the City Planning Department do not show the Alviso area as archaeologically sensitive. However, in view of the information provided by Mr. Ogilvie, the mitigation measures provided in the Summary Section (K. Cultural Resources p. viii) the last sentence should be modified to read: Consultation with a qualified archaeologist should precede all excavations for sewer lines and building foundations in the Alviso/CNRA and in those portions of the target area identified on the Archaeological Sensitivity Maps on file in the Planning Department, City of San Jose.
<u>Comment</u>: The 20 residential structures scheduled for demolition must be assessed for their architecture, historic, or engineering significance.
Response: Mitigation measures under Section K, Cultural Resources, page viii, addresses this comment adequately.
Comment: The Office of Historical Preservation would appreciate an opportunity to review and comment on the EIR/EIS prepared for the Block Grant Program.
Response: The Office of Historical Preservation is furnished a copy by the State Clearinghouse, to which we furnished five (5) copies.
Response to comments from Gene Saalwaechter, Director of Parks and Recreation, is on errata sheet.
Response to comment from Gordon Schmelzer is on errata sheet.
